prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After reading all eight first-round statements and my own chair summary, I keep B015 as a single-part prize with Katori and Ye, and the exchange has made my reasons more specific. The novelty question that nearly every member raised has a concrete answer. The 2005 prize honoured the comb, a way to count optical cycles, and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped quantum systems, including ion clocks. Neither introduced a trapping scheme in which the light shift cancels for the clock transition, so that a large ensemble of neutral atoms can be interrogated at once. That condition is what moved neutral-atom clocks from a promising idea to systematic uncertainty and stability at the 1e-18 level, and the stability gain from interrogating many atoms is part of what ion clocks cannot match. Independent reproduction and intercomparison in several laboratories is the evidence that the calibration and systematics are sound, which is the test I apply as an experimentalist. On credit, I read Katori's proposal of the magic-wavelength lattice and his first strontium clock as the originating idea, and Ye's work as taking the scheme to record accuracy and stability and introducing many-body clock physics. The citation can say 'invention and realization' without claiming that either name alone created the clock family. The citation does not rest on the redefinition of the second, which is supporting context and not a condition. Eight of eight members ranked B015 and all eight named the same two people; no dissenter called it unacceptable. I have not changed my configuration since round 1, and I have not been moved by the support count itself. What moved me in round 1 was that the credit for this entry is the most defensible on the list.
statement.case_against: The reservations remain real. A third prize in frequency metrology after 2005 and 2012 can be read as incremental, and this is an invention with a precision payoff more than a discovery of an unexpected phenomenon; Danielsson's discovery-first principle is a legitimate criterion that I do not dismiss. The strongest fundamental-physics results from clocks so far are null results that tighten bounds, as Kroll notes, and the redefinition of the second has not yet taken place, so the practical payoff is still prospective. Ion clocks, such as Al+ systems, reach comparable uncertainty and Lindroth is right that they remain a strong rival line, which means the citation has to be written about the lattice scheme and not about optical clocks in general. Finally, the groups at PTB, NIST, SYRTE, RIKEN and elsewhere contributed to the neutral-atom clocks. I read that as confirmation, but a citation that suggests the lattice clock had a single origin would invite fair criticism.

responses.point: Kroll asked that the B015 citation be worded so as not to imply a single origin of the clock family, and raised a two-part configuration pairing the clock with a measurement-driven discovery such as B007 or B057.
responses.response: I accept the wording point and have written my citation around the invention and realization of the lattice clock with magic-wavelength trapping, not around atomic clocks in general. On the two-part idea, I looked at it seriously and I do not support it. The three-person limit means a second part would have to carry at most one name alongside Katori and Ye, which cannot be done for B007 without dropping Halzen, Karle or Spiering and cannot be done for B057, where the credit among Pritchard, Mlynek, Kasevich and the uncredited Chu and Borde is the least settled on the list. Pairing a clean part with an unclean one would weaken both. I would rather vote the clean single prize now and keep IceCube for a year in which its three names can be defended.

responses.point: Danielsson argued that IceCube is a clue from nature, that its source identification need not delay recognition, and that Halzen, Karle and Spiering is a workable allocation, while conceding that B015 is the safer choice and that B007 gets less support among colleagues.
responses.response: I agree that the diffuse flux is a discovery in the strict sense and that TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 do not need independent confirmation by KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD for the flux itself to stand; I put IceCube first in my opening for that reason. Our remaining difference is the third name. You asked whether Spiering's role in AMANDA and the discovery analysis is decisive, and I cannot say it is more decisive than the roles of other IceCube analysis and detector leaders; I proposed him on the strength of the AMANDA-to-IceCube continuity. Because that is a judgement I cannot defend against Olsson's Halzen and Karle pair, I am not willing to let a split on that name hold back B015. You also called B015 the safer choice, and I take that seriously. My test is that the physics is mature and the credit is clear, and that is why I rank B007 as my first alternative and not as my preferred part.

responses.point: Olsson asked whether Ye's role is the original invention or a later, higher-performance realization of Katori's scheme, and proposed only Halzen and Karle for IceCube.
responses.response: Your question about Ye is the central credit question for B015, and I think both readings are partly right. I treat Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium clock as the originating step, and Ye's realization as the one that turned the scheme into a record-setting system and brought in many-body effects, with the stability gain from large atom numbers. Both belong in a citation that says 'invention and realization'. If you or Lindroth can name an early lattice proposal that predates Katori's, that would change my view and I would want to hear it before the ballot. On IceCube, your two-name version is the cleaner of the two proposals from a credit standpoint, and your answer on B013 is that you now treat it as a fallback; I will say again that I do not treat instrumentation as lesser, but I cannot support B013 while Krivanek and Dellby remain outside the three names.

responses.point: Eriksson said he would not stand in the way of B015 if the committee judges B006 to be early, and set B006's main risk as the unsettled pairing mechanism and the missing experimental first author Cao.
responses.response: Thank you; your concession matters, and I do not read it as a lukewarm one. On B006 I accept that the single-particle flat band is secure and that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 experiments is the clearest theory-then-experiment chain on the list. What I cannot judge, and what I rely on you and Mehlig for, is whether a prize can be written that rests on the flat-band prediction and the discovery of correlated phases without implying a view on pairing. Even if it can, the three-name limit leaves out Cao and the independent groups, and I would not want to resolve that under time pressure. If B015 does not carry, B006 is my second alternative and I would revisit it with you.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B015 with the condition that other laboratories confirm rather than compete for credit, but also noted that Al+ ion clocks are a rival line at similar uncertainty and that Katori's proposal and Ye's accuracy are not the whole story.
responses.response: I agree with the rival-line point and think it sharpens the citation. Ion clocks reaching similar uncertainty does not reduce the lattice clock's contribution, because the magic-wavelength condition is about interrogating many neutral atoms and the achievable stability. It does mean the citation must not say that the lattice clock is the only route to the 1e-18 level. On the redefinition of the second, we are close: I want it outside the citation, as supporting context. If the General Conference slips, the physics case is unchanged and only the societal argument weakens, so a prize now does not depend on its outcome.

responses.point: Mehlig argued that B006 honours a secure flat-band mechanism and an experimental discovery, that the unsettled pairing mechanism is not a reason to delay, and that B015 has the cleaner attribution and stronger agreement.
responses.response: I take your argument that a prize can honour the flat-band prediction and the discovery of correlated states without waiting for the pairing mechanism. I cannot judge that from my own field and I am not dismissing it. Your own statement concedes that B015 has cleaner attribution and stronger agreement among colleagues, and that is the factor I weigh most this year, together with the open questions about Bistritzer's share and about Cao. I have kept B006 as my second alternative and not removed it, and I would like to hear whether you and Eriksson regard the Cao and independent-group problem as soluble within three names, since that, and not the physics, is what keeps me from ranking it first.

uncertainties: Whether any early lattice-clock proposal predates Katori's magic-wavelength scheme or affects the split of credit with Ye; I am working from memory and have not verified priority.
Whether members who prefer B007 or B006 regard the novelty relative to 2005 and 2012 as settled by the magic-wavelength argument, or still see B015 as incremental.
Whether the Halzen, Karle and Spiering allocation for IceCube can be settled in a later year, and whether Spiering's role is decisive.
Whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second; I treat it as outside the citation, but members differ.
My limited expertise in condensed matter and quantum information means I defer to Eriksson, Mehlig, Johansson and Lindroth on B006, B055 and B024.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B015 and no connection to Katori, Ye or the optical clock groups. For B007 I repeat that IceCube is a neighbouring astroparticle collaboration and I work in PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur; this is community proximity, with no tie to the credited names, and I do not propose recusal. As Chair I note that Johansson (B024), Olsson (B013) and Kroll (JILA lineage with Ye's institute) have disclosed connections in round 1; I take them as stated and see no reason to ask for recusal on B015, but I would ask Kroll to confirm that his JILA lineage has no bearing on his vote on B015.
